title: Rasterize
description: Rasterize is the 2004 album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of metalcore about how computers turn numbers into pictures. Nyble sings the clean choruses and plays bass, Qword is finally allowed guitar solos again, Wyrd adds atmospheric synths, and Bytes plays double-kick drums and screams the backing vocals. Bresenham’s line algorithm, RGB color, triangles, matrix transforms, perspective, the graphics pipeline, the z-buffer, Phong lighting, texture mapping, anti-aliasing, ray tracing and animation. Written while Wyrd built the band’s first 3D music video by hand. Null was modeled with twelve triangles, and the fans liked it better. Play loud. Sixty frames a second.
tagline: The 2004 metalcore album from Procedural Byts: a computer graphics course in twelve songs, starting with a single straight line.
lineup: The four-piece, rendered in 3D. Nyble sings clean lead vocals on every song and plays bass guitar. Qword plays lead guitar and solos again. Wyrd plays atmospheric synths. Bytes plays drums and screams the backing vocals.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits, and the clean voice against Bytes’s screams. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass, and in the music video she was rendered with twelve hundred triangles, which she says was about right.

members.name: Qword
members.bio: Sixty-four bits, and allowed to play guitar solos again for the first time since 1989. Qword has a solo on nearly every song on this album and has not stopped smiling.

members.name: Wyrd
members.bio: Thirty-two bits, on atmospheric synths, and the one who built the band’s 3D music video by hand, one matrix at a time. Wyrd also modeled the duck, in a hurry.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, double-kick drums, and as of 2004 the band’s screamer. He asked to be scaled up in the music video. The request was denied.

members.name: Null
members.bio: Twelve triangles. The band’s logo since 2004.

story.heading: Twelve Triangles
paragraphs: In 2004, metalcore arrived, and the band changed shape again. Nyble kept singing the clean, soaring choruses. Bytes discovered he could scream, which the rest of the band had suspected for years. And Qword was told, for the first time since 1989, that guitar solos were back. Qword cried, briefly, then played one on nearly every song.

The label wanted a music video, and Wyrd decided to build it in 3D, by hand. The first thing Wyrd ever drew on a computer screen, back in 1985, was a single straight line using Bresenham’s algorithm. So that is where the album starts.

Every member was modeled out of triangles, moved and spun by matrices, lit, textured and rendered. The first render was a disaster. Bytes appeared in front of Nyble, through his own drum kit, because nothing knew which surface was closer. Qword’s guitar had edges like a staircase. Those two bugs became Z-Buffer and Jaggies.

Wyrd ran out of time before modeling Null and built the duck from just twelve triangles. The fans loved it. The low-poly duck has been the band’s logo ever since, and it outsold the real duck at the merch table.
The final shot was ray traced across four computers and took three weeks, which the band only knew how to split up because of what they learned in 2001. The duck rendered in under a second.

songs.title: Bresenham

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A screen is just a grid of squares, no curves and no between,
Draw a line from here to there across the pixel screen.
Step along the x one square at a time,
And choose the pixel closest to the line!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Bresenham! (Step by step!)
Bresenham! (Error kept!)
Add the slope to the error, and when it’s more than half you climb,
Bresenham, Bresenham, integers every time!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: No floating point, no division, nothing but add and compare,
Nineteen sixty-two, a plotter pen moving through the air.
Keep a running error of how far the line has strayed,
When it tips past the middle, take a step up, and the line is made!

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)
lines: Step x! (Add dy!)
Too far? (Step y!)
Subtract dx! (And try again!)
Pixel by pixel to the end!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword’s first real solo since 1989 climbs the neck like a line on a screen: a few notes across, then one step up, then across again, with the steps spaced exactly to match the slope.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Bresenham! (Step by step!)
Bresenham! (Error kept!)
Add the slope to the error, and when it’s more than half you climb,
Bresenham, Bresenham, integers every time!

songs.note: The first thing Wyrd ever drew on a computer screen, back in 1985, was a single straight line. The album starts there because everything on a screen does.
songs.lesson: A screen is a grid of pixels, so a line has to be approximated by choosing which pixels to light. Bresenham’s line algorithm (1962, written for IBM plotters) steps one pixel at a time along the longer axis and keeps a running integer error. When the error passes the halfway point, it also steps along the shorter axis and subtracts. It uses only integer addition and comparison, with no floating point and no division, which made it fast on early hardware.

songs.title: RGB

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Red and green and blue of light, the only paint I need,
Add them up together and the white light is freed.
Turn them all to zero and the screen goes black as night,
Every color in between is just a mix of light!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: R! G! B! (Red, green, blue!)
Three numbers make every color that comes through!
Two fifty-five of each and the brightest white you’ll see,
R, G, B, every pixel’s made of three!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Eight bits for every channel, sixteen million in all,
The framebuffer holds a number for each pixel on the wall.
Resolution is how many, depth is how much each can hold,
Mix the light and not the paint, and that’s the story told!

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)
lines: Additive! (Light!) Not subtractive! (Paint!)
All three at once! (White!) None at all! (Night!)

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd plays three synth lines, one red, one green and one blue, each alone at first. As they overlap they blend into new chords, and when all three play at full volume, it’s white.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: R! G! B! (Red, green, blue!)
Three numbers make every color that comes through!
Two fifty-five of each and the brightest white you’ll see,
R, G, B, every pixel’s made of three!

songs.note: Every color on the album cover is listed in the liner notes as three numbers.
songs.lesson: Screens mix light, not paint, so color is additive: red, green and blue (RGB) combine to make every color, with all three at full brightness giving white and none giving black. A common format uses 8 bits per channel, values from 0 to 255, for about 16.7 million colors. The framebuffer holds a color for every pixel; resolution is how many pixels there are, and color depth is how many bits each one gets.

songs.title: Made of Triangles

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The dragon and the castle and the face upon the screen,
Up close it’s only triangles, the flattest shapes you’ve seen.
Three points always make a plane, it never bends or breaks,
Build anything from triangles and see what shape it takes!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Made of triangles! (Three points!)
Made of triangles! (Every joint!)
A mesh of tiny faces, every curve a lie,
Made of triangles, made of triangles, and it fools the eye!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Fill it in row by row, scan conversion line by line,
Inside or outside of the edges, test it every time.
Blend the corners’ colors with barycentric weights,
And the middle gets the mixture that the corners create!

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)
lines: More triangles! (Smoother!) Fewer triangles! (Faster!)
Twelve triangles! (The duck!) And the duck’s the master!

parts.label: Interlocking chords: Qword and Nyble
parts.desc: The solo is built only from three-note chords. Qword and Nyble lock them together edge to edge, one after another, until the shape of the main riff appears out of nothing but triangles.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Made of triangles! (Three points!)
Made of triangles! (Every joint!)
A mesh of tiny faces, every curve a lie,
Made of triangles, made of triangles, and it fools the eye!

songs.note: Null was modeled with twelve triangles in the music video. The fans liked the low-poly duck better than the real one.
songs.lesson: 3D models are usually meshes of triangles, because three points always lie on one flat plane. Rasterization, also called scan conversion, fills each triangle by working out which pixels fall inside its three edges. Values stored at the corners, like color, depth and texture coordinates, are blended across the inside using barycentric coordinates. More triangles look smoother but take longer to draw.

songs.title: Matrix Transform

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Move it to the left, that’s a translation,
Spin it round the middle, that’s a rotation,
Make it twice as big, that’s a scale for you,
Every one’s a matrix, and the matrix moves it through!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Matrix transform! (Multiply!)
Matrix transform! (Watch it fly!)
Four by four, and one more coordinate on top,
Matrix transform, transform, and the vertices hop!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Add a one to every point, homogeneous and wide,
Now translation is a multiply, with rotation side by side.
Combine them in one matrix, but the order’s not the same,
Rotate then move, or move then rotate, it’s a different game!

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)
lines: Translate! Rotate! Scale!
Order matters, or the transform fails!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays one short phrase, then transforms it: moves it up the neck (translate), turns it upside down (rotate), and stretches it to double length (scale). Then Qword plays all three in the wrong order, and it comes out as a completely different phrase.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Matrix transform! (Multiply!)
Matrix transform! (Watch it fly!)
Four by four, and one more coordinate on top,
Matrix transform, transform, and the vertices hop!

songs.note: In the music video, every member was moved, spun and scaled by a matrix. Bytes asked to be scaled up. The request was denied.
songs.lesson: Transformations move geometry around: translation moves it, rotation spins it and scaling resizes it. With homogeneous coordinates, where every point gets an extra fourth coordinate of 1, all three, including translation, become 4×4 matrix multiplications, so a whole chain of them can be combined into a single matrix. Matrix multiplication isn’t commutative, so the order of transformations matters.

songs.title: Perspective

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Far away is small and close up is large,
The railway lines converge, and the horizon’s in charge.
Put the eye at the center with the world out in front,
Divide by the distance, that’s the perspective stunt!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Perspective! (Divide by z!)
Perspective! (What the eye can see!)
Near plane, far plane, the frustum in between,
Perspective, perspective, and the world is on the screen!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The camera has a position and a place it’s looking at,
Move the whole world to the camera, then flatten it out flat.
Orthographic keeps the size the same no matter how far,
Perspective shrinks the distant, and it shows you where you are!

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)
lines: Closer! (Bigger!) Further! (Smaller!)
Vanishing point! (Everything falls in!)

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd’s synth line starts tiny and distant in the middle of the mix and grows louder and wider as it approaches, until by the end it fills both speakers: something flying toward the camera.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Perspective! (Divide by z!)
Perspective! (What the eye can see!)
Near plane, far plane, the frustum in between,
Perspective, perspective, and the world is on the screen!

songs.note: The music video’s camera starts in the back row of the crowd and flies toward the stage. Everything gets bigger. That’s the song.
songs.lesson: To draw a 3D scene you place a virtual camera, transform the world into the camera’s point of view, and project it onto a flat image. Perspective projection divides by depth, so distant things look smaller and parallel lines meet at a vanishing point; orthographic projection keeps sizes the same at every distance. The view frustum, cut off by a near and a far plane, is everything the camera can see.

songs.title: The Pipeline

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Vertices come in at the top of the line,
Transform them to the screen, every corner every time.
Assemble them to triangles, rasterize to fragments small,
Shade them, test them, blend them, and then write them to the wall!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: The pipeline! (Stage by stage!)
The pipeline! (Down the line!)
Millions of triangles flowing through in parallel time,
The pipeline, the pipeline, and every frame is mine!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The graphics card does this in parallel, a thousand at a go,
Vertex shader, fragment shader, programs we now know.
Write a little program for each corner, each pixel too,
The GPU runs them all at once, and the frame comes through!

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)
lines: Vertex! Raster! Fragment! Output!
Every stage in parallel! Now shout it!

parts.label: Down the line: full band
parts.desc: Bytes starts the riff, Nyble transforms it, Wyrd fills it in and Qword colors it, each stage already working on the next riff while the one before is still moving through.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: The pipeline! (Stage by stage!)
The pipeline! (Down the line!)
Millions of triangles flowing through in parallel time,
The pipeline, the pipeline, and every frame is mine!

songs.note: In 2004, graphics cards had just become programmable. The band recorded this one standing in a row, passing each part down the line.
songs.lesson: The graphics pipeline turns 3D geometry into pixels in stages: transform each vertex, assemble vertices into triangles, rasterize triangles into fragments (candidate pixels), shade and texture each fragment, then depth-test and blend the results into the framebuffer. GPUs run these stages massively in parallel, and by the early 2000s the vertex and fragment stages had become programmable through small programs called shaders.

songs.title: Z-Buffer

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Draw them in any order and the far ones cover the near,
The drummer’s in front of the singer and the stage is out of here.
Who should we see? Whoever’s closest to the eye,
Keep a depth for every pixel, and only nearest ones get by!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Z-buffer! (Who’s in front?)
Z-buffer! (Closest wins the hunt!)
Test the depth of every pixel before you paint it on,
Z-buffer, z-buffer, and the hidden ones are gone!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The painter sorts them back to front and paints the near ones last,
But overlapping triangles won’t sort, and that idea is past.
The z-buffer doesn’t care what order they arrive,
Compare the depth, keep the closest, and the picture comes alive!

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)
lines: Nearer? (Draw it!) Farther? (Drop it!)
Every pixel! (Test it!) Hidden surface! (Stop it!)

parts.label: Front of the mix: Qword and Nyble
parts.desc: Qword and Nyble play overlapping parts, and at each moment the engineer lets through only whichever one is closer to the front of the mix. The other part is still there, just hidden behind.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Z-buffer! (Who’s in front?)
Z-buffer! (Closest wins the hunt!)
Test the depth of every pixel before you paint it on,
Z-buffer, z-buffer, and the hidden ones are gone!

songs.note: In the first render of the music video, Bytes appeared in front of Nyble, through his own drum kit. This song fixed it.
songs.lesson: When surfaces overlap, only the nearest one should show. The painter’s algorithm sorts surfaces and draws them back to front, but fails when surfaces overlap each other in a cycle. The z-buffer, or depth buffer, stores the depth of the nearest surface drawn so far at every pixel, and a new fragment is drawn only if it’s closer. Triangles can then arrive in any order.

songs.title: Phong

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Without any light, a sphere is just a disc of grey,
Shade it by its angle to the light and it comes into the day.
Facing the light is bright, and turned away is dim,
The normal points out from the surface, and the light pours in!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Ambient! (The glow!)
Diffuse! (The matte below!)
Specular! (The shine!)
Add them up, and the light is mine!
Phong, Phong, the highlight burns so bright,
Phong, Phong, and the world is full of light!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Ambient is the light from everywhere, a dim and even base,
Diffuse depends upon the angle, soft across the face.
Specular’s the highlight where the light reflects to you,
Shiny things get a small sharp spot, and matte ones never do!

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)
lines: Flat shading! (One color per face!)
Smooth shading! (Blend it all over the place!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword’s solo starts with soft, even notes (ambient), swells as it turns toward the light (diffuse), and peaks on one piercing high note held for a full bar: the specular highlight.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Ambient! (The glow!)
Diffuse! (The matte below!)
Specular! (The shine!)
Add them up, and the light is mine!
Phong, Phong, the highlight burns so bright,
Phong, Phong, and the world is full of light!

songs.note: Named after Bui Tuong Phong, who invented this lighting model in 1975. The highlight in the solo is the highest note on the album.
songs.lesson: Lighting models work out a surface’s color from the lights, the direction the surface faces (its normal) and where the viewer is. The Phong reflection model (1975) adds three parts: ambient (an even base glow), diffuse (brighter the more the surface faces the light, giving a matte look) and specular (a shiny highlight where light reflects toward the viewer). Flat shading uses one color per triangle, Gouraud shading blends corner colors, and Phong shading blends normals and lights every pixel.

songs.title: Texture

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A box is just a box until you wrap it up in skin,
Paste a picture of some bricks, and now it’s a wall you’re in.
Give every corner coordinates, a U and then a V,
They tell you where to sample from the picture that you see!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Texture! (Wrap it around!)
Texture! (Detail found!)
A picture on the surface makes a thousand triangles real,
Texture, texture, and it’s something you can almost feel!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Look at it from far away and the texture starts to shimmer,
Too many texels in a pixel, and they flicker and they glimmer.
So make some smaller copies, mipmaps for the distance,
Pick the size that fits, and the flicker loses its insistence!

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)
lines: U! (Across!) V! (Up!)
Sample the picture! (Paint it up!)

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd takes the simplest possible melody, three notes, and wraps it in layer after layer of sampled sound. The notes never change; the surface does, until three notes sound like an orchestra.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Texture! (Wrap it around!)
Texture! (Detail found!)
A picture on the surface makes a thousand triangles real,
Texture, texture, and it’s something you can almost feel!

songs.note: Every member’s face in the video was a photograph wrapped around twelve hundred triangles. Null’s was a photograph wrapped around twelve.
songs.lesson: Texture mapping adds detail by wrapping an image around geometry. Each vertex gets texture coordinates, u and v, which are blended across the triangle so every pixel knows where to sample the image. Seen from far away, a texture can shimmer because too much of it squeezes into each pixel, so mipmapping stores smaller, pre-filtered copies and picks the size that fits.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A diagonal edge on a grid of square light,

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays the solo twice. The first time, every note is chopped short and square: a staircase. The second time it’s the same notes, sampled four times as often and blended, and the line comes out smooth.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Jaggies! (Staircase edge!)
Jaggies! (Off the ledge!)
Sample more than once a pixel and average what you see,
Anti-aliasing, smooth it out for me!

songs.note: In the first render, Qword’s guitar had edges like a staircase. Qword took it personally.
songs.lesson: Aliasing happens when an image has more detail than the pixel grid can capture: jagged staircase edges (“jaggies”), edges that crawl when things move, strange moiré patterns, or wagon wheels that seem to spin backwards on film. Anti-aliasing takes several samples per pixel and averages them (supersampling), or filters before sampling, so edge pixels get in-between colors and look smooth.

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays one phrase, and it reflects back quieter, then quieter again, each echo a bounce, until it fades into the dark. The base case ends the solo, the same way it ended CS1.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Ray tracer! (Follow the light!)
Ray tracer! (Bounce it right!)
Reflection, refraction, shadows true and deep,
Ray tracer, ray tracer, every ray’s a leap!

songs.note: The music video’s final shot was ray traced. It took four computers three weeks. The band only knew how to split it up because of 2001.
songs.lesson: Ray tracing draws a picture by shooting a ray from the eye through each pixel, finding the nearest surface it hits, and then shooting more rays: one toward each light to check for shadow, and reflected and refracted rays that bounce on recursively until a depth limit stops them, the base case. It produces accurate shadows, reflections and glass, but it’s expensive, so in 2004 real-time graphics used rasterization instead.

songs.title: Sixty Frames

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Show a picture, show another, change it just a bit,
Sixty times a second and the eye believes in it.
Every frame is drawn behind the screen where you can’t see,

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Sixty frames! (Every second!)
Sixty frames! (Motion beckoned!)
Draw it, swap it, draw again, and never let it tear,
Sixty frames, sixty frames, and it’s alive out there!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Keyframes at the moments where the motion starts and stops,
Interpolate between them and the animation pops.
Read the input, update the world, and draw it all once more,

parts.label: Bridge (screamed)
lines: Sixteen milliseconds! (That’s all you get!)
Miss the deadline! (Drop the frame!) Don’t forget!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword’s final solo is fast, but every note lands exactly on a sixteenth-note grid, like frames on a clock. Then the whole band swaps in at once, like a buffer flipping to the front, and the album ends on the downbeat.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Sixty frames! (Every second!)
Sixty frames! (Motion beckoned!)
Draw it, swap it, draw again, and never let it tear,
Sixty frames, sixty frames, and it’s alive out there!

songs.note: The music video ran at sixty frames per second. The duck, at twelve triangles, finished rendering before each frame had even started.
songs.lesson: Animation is a sequence of still frames shown fast enough to look like motion, typically 24 to 60 or more per second; at 60 frames per second, each frame gets about 16.7 milliseconds. Double buffering draws the next frame into a hidden back buffer, then swaps it to the screen all at once to avoid flicker and tearing. Keyframe animation sets key poses and interpolates between them, and interactive programs run a loop: read input, update the world, render.
